<reason>A builds the stronger comparative case: mandatory testing and disclosure can inform decisions before harm without guaranteeing safety or replacing liability. A answers both pressure questions directly, including the difficult concession that adverse findings do not automatically block deployment. B raises legitimate concerns about comparability, compliance costs, and false reassurance, but overstates them into unsupported claims that redacted reporting conveys nothing and mandatory evaluation necessarily means clearance. A’s preventive-information mechanism survives those attacks, while B concedes its alternative does not compel pre-launch disclosure.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A’s closing resolves B’s alleged contradiction about reputation: mandatory publication moves scrutiny before harm, whereas the opening criticized punishment arriving afterward. A also correctly rejects the “warning into a waiver” claim because disclosure creates no exemption from liability. Together, these answers defeat B’s strongest attack on the proposal’s preventive value.</best_rebuttal>
